1.pericope_label: Now it came to pass in the thirtieth year, in the fourth month, in the fifth day of the month, as I was among the captives by the river of Chebar, that the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God
debates: What the thirtieth year is reckoned from
Why the prophet speaks of himself in the third person
Whether the father named was a prophet
outliers: Five reckonings of the thirtieth year are offered: from the last jubilee, from the finding of the book of the law, from the age of the prophet, from the accession of the father of Nebuchadnezzar, and by Ellicott from the epoch shared with the captivity of the king
Calvin rejects the reckoning from the finding of the law as too obscure and forced and unsupported by later writers, and argues for the jubilee
Ellicott suggests the third person and the naming of himself may indicate these verses were inserted on a revision of the work by the prophet
Calvin dismisses the identification of the father with Jeremiah as resting only on a persuasion that the father of a prophet must himself be one
themes: A man in exile dating by the reckoning of the country he is in, as men abroad use the new style
Exiles more than exiles but less than prisoners
A sabbath supposed because the people were at leisure to hear
A caution that the prophet is portraying what exceeds the power of human language

4.pericope_label: And I looked, and, behold, a whirlwind came out of the north, a great cloud, and a fire infolding itself, and a brightness was about it
debates: Why the vision comes from the north
What the four living creatures signify
Whether the creatures may be named yet
outliers: Clarke and Wesley take the north simply for Babylon; Ellicott denies any Babylonian notion of a northern seat of divine power and explains it by prophetic usage and the route of invasion
Calvin rejects four readings of the creatures in turn, as the seasons, as four virtues, as four passions or faculties, and as the four Evangelists, and holds them to be angels

Ellicott holds back from naming them here, since the prophet only recognised them as the cherubim in a later vision, and stresses that the word likeness marks them as symbolic rather than actually existing creatures
Ellicott reports that transposing a single letter would make the whirlwind bring on the cloud rather than accompany it
themes: A God who has power to pursue a servant who draws back, as he did Jonah
A word rendered amber used of a bright metal compounded of gold and brass
Flashes so rapid that each seemed to lay hold on the one before
A cloud serving at once as groundwork and as hiding place, so that what the eye cannot bear is still known to be there

6.pericope_label: And every one had four faces, and every one had four wings. And their feet were straight feet; and the sole of their feet was like the sole of a calf foot
debates: How many heads and wings each creature had
What the hands under the wings represent
Whether the creatures figure angels or ministers
outliers: Calvin rejects the readings that give each animal four heads with four appearances apiece, or four wings to every head, or sixteen wings, holding that heads and wings correspond at four each
Ellicott treats the numbers as of no great weight, since the cherubim are variously represented elsewhere with one face or two and with two wings or six
Clarke suspects the arms were feathered so as to look like wings with only the hand bare, where Ellicott infers from the four hands that the wings were attached at the shoulder
Gill alone reads the figure allegorically of the ministers of the Gospel rather than of angels
themes: Ancient images whose gods glide rather than walk, offered as a criterion for telling gods from other spirits
A poet quoted for the erect posture that distinguishes man from the brutes
A round foot able to move in any direction where a man turning must contend with nature
A hundred hands given by the poets to a man of business

9.pericope_label: Their wings were joined one to another; they turned not when they went; they went every one straight forward
debates: Whether the wings were stretched upward or separated above
Why a later vision puts a cherub where this one puts an ox
How the creatures could change course without turning
outliers: Ellicott holds the word never means stretched but always separated or divided, against the versions Gill reports, which render both faces and wings stretched upwards

Calvin rejects the answer that the face looked like an ox at a distance and a cherub nearer as a sophistry, rejects the identification of cherub with ox, and concludes the second vision differed in this particular
Ellicott answers the objection that covering wings would have to turn by arranging the four in a square moving as one creature
Calvin holds going straight forward is not contradicted by running like lightning and returning, since they proceed in a perpetual course without resting at the goal
themes: Extended wings forming a canopy on which the throne rested
Wings that soared without flapping, as the feet glided without walking
Compound idols with eight arms or six heads, symbolical and each with a meaning now lost
Confusion on earth resolving into harmony to one who raises his eyes to heaven

12.pericope_label: And they went every one straight forward: whither the spirit was to go, they went; and they turned not when they went
debates: What the spirit that moved them is
Whether the appearance of lamps is a second thing or an explanation
What the running and returning describes
outliers: Four readings of the spirit are given: Clarke the whirlwind, Ellicott one informing spirit animating the creatures, Wesley the Spirit of God, and Calvin the will or mind, expressly against the senses of wind and of the human soul
Ellicott removes a conjunction not in the original so that the lamps explain the burning coals rather than adding to them, and holds that lamps names the light and not the material

Clarke reads the running and returning as a circular movement that never increased their distance from the spectator, where Calvin reads it as a course that does not turn back before the goal is reached
Wesley holds that moving itself is too much to ascribe to creatures, God alone moving them
themes: Sparks like those struck from ignited iron in a forge, and warring wheels in pyrotechny
A prophet who could find no single word and gave two
A bush that would not have arrested Moses had it burned and been consumed
Souls told to return from the affairs of this world like lightning

15.pericope_label: Now as I beheld the living creatures, behold one wheel upon the earth by the living creatures, with his four faces
debates: What a wheel in the middle of a wheel means
What stone the colour is taken from
Whether one likeness refers to the wheels or the creatures
outliers: Clarke rejects the usual reading of two wheels cutting at right angles and takes the wheel within for the nave in which the spokes are inserted, reporting that models built to move equally in all directions cannot do so
Ellicott and Wesley hold the double wheel at right angles, Ellicott granting that such a wheel would be mechanically impossible and was never intended to be made

Gill names the beryl and reports the Syriac chrysolite and the Arabic jasper; Ellicott denies our beryl is meant and identifies the chrysolite of the ancients, the modern topaz; Calvin rejects the sea colour of Jerome and declines to identify the stone at all
Ellicott rejects deriving the imagery from the wheels under the bases of the temple of Solomon, holding it purely original
themes: Providence compared to a clock whose parts all contribute to the regular motion
A wheel whose spokes rise and fall while the axle turns steadily
Drawings in which deities walk upon wheels encompassed with fire
A prophet convicted of infirmity because he could not embrace the vision at once

18.pericope_label: As for their rings, they were so high that they were dreadful; and their rings were full of eyes round about them four
debates: What the eyes on the rims are
Whether the wheels had life of their own
Whether the height caused the dreadfulness
outliers: Clarke suggests the eyes may be the appearance of nails holding the spokes or the bands upon the rim, where Calvin takes them for a providence that never wanders and Ellicott for the perfect knowledge God has of his works
Clarke holds the wheels were instinct with a vital spirit and were themselves animals; Calvin denies them any motion of their own, and Wesley calls them inferior agents and second causes
Ellicott corrects the English rendering, holding high and terrible to be two characteristics rather than the one causing the other
Gill reports a rendering that gives the wheels fear rather than dreadfulness, a reverence in themselves
themes: A wheel so great that looking from the ground to the top was tremendous
Eyes fixed on the felloes because anywhere else they would be useless
The whole vision assembled into a chariot with a canopy of wings
Angels said to be discharging their duty when things fall out unseasonably

21.pericope_label: And the likeness of the firmament upon the heads of the living creature was as the colour of the terrible crystal, stretched forth over their heads above
debates: Whether the living creatures can be angels
What the word rendered firmament means
How the terrible crystal should be rendered
outliers: Gill argues from the firmament being over their heads that the creatures cannot be angels, whose habitation is above it, nor a figure of the three Persons, and must be ministers of the Gospel; Calvin and Wesley take them for angels throughout
Ellicott traces the word to a verb meaning to beat out but denies the derivative kept that sense, and denies that the Hebrews held the classical idea of a metallic vault
Clarke reports a rendering that gives fearful ice and prefers the common translation; Ellicott denies that any particular crystal is meant at all
Calvin holds the wheels only receive vigour and comprehend nothing, as the moon takes its brightness from the sun
themes: A wheel standing still on its rim, which nature does not allow
An expanse that stayed undisturbed when the wings were let down
The firmament doing above what the wheels do below, joining the vision to God as they join it to earth
Stages set by which a prophet might climb to an immense altitude

23.pericope_label: And when they went, I heard the noise of their wings, like the noise of great waters, as the voice of the Almighty, the voice of speech, as the noise of an host
debates: Whether the voice was articulate
What the upper wings were for
How the covering wings should be counted
outliers: Ellicott holds every comparison represents a sound vast and terrible but inarticulate, the voice of speech naming the confused sound of a multitude; Wesley holds the prophet heard the voice in an articulate manner
Clarke makes the upper wings a foundation for the firmament to rest on, which Ellicott denies, holding the expanse neither supported by the creatures nor resting on them
Ellicott blames the literalness of the English for seeming to give each cherub four covering wings instead of two; Calvin rejects as absurd the view that makes the upper and lower pairs the same
Ellicott would render the word voice throughout rather than noise three times and voice twice
themes: A sound compared to a waterfall and to waters dashing against rocks
Wheels said to obey without being endued with ears
An overflowing river whose crash seems to threaten the breaking up of things
Creatures presenting themselves before God once their office is done

25.pericope_label: And there was a voice from the firmament that was over their heads, when they stood, and had let down their wings
debates: Where the voice came from
Whether the last clause repeats the preceding verse
To whom the likeness of a man may be applied
outliers: Ellicott corrects the preposition, holding the voice came from above the firmament rather than proceeding from the firmament itself
Ellicott allows the last clause may simply repeat the end of the preceding verse but prefers to read a fresh act of reverence at the sound of the voice

Calvin rejects the reading of Jerome that applies the words to the Father, since the Father was never clad in flesh, and holds the likeness of a man can be transferred neither to the Father nor to the Spirit
Calvin denies that what was seen was the true heavens, or a throne of material substance, or a real body, and holds appearance is joined to likeness to exclude any visible form in God
themes: A voice at which the sounds of their going were hushed and the wings fell motionless
A vision summed up in stages, from the whirlwind to the throne
A form of man called a prelude to the mystery afterwards displayed
A christology rejected in which the flesh was absorbed by the deity until no trace of human nature remained

26.pericope_label: And above the firmament that was over their heads was the likeness of a throne, as the appearance of a sapphire stone: and upon the likeness of the throne was the likeness as the appearance of a man above upon it
debates: Who the man upon the throne is
What the word rendered amber means
Whether the vision hints at the incarnation
outliers: Henry, Clarke and Wesley identify the man upon the throne with Christ; Ellicott denies that the Divine Being himself was seen and holds the appearances were given only to impress his character and attributes

Calvin rejects a rendering that finds an angel in the word and holds a colour is meant, and calls foolish the claim of Jerome that the substance is more precious than gold and silver, since it is composed of both
Ellicott allows only that there may possibly be a hint of the incarnation, where Clarke states it plainly and Henry builds a whole argument on it
Ellicott takes the fivefold repetition of likeness and appearance in one verse as the labour of the prophet to mark the vision as symbolic rather than real
themes: The heads of angels said to lie under the feet of the Lord Jesus
A sapphire and a specimen of amber held up to the light by the commentator
Eyes that can distinguish the parts of a man or a tree but are dimmed by the sun
Garments of salvation exchanged for garments of vengeance

28.pericope_label: As the appearance of the bow that is in the cloud in the day of rain, so was the appearance of the brightness round about. This was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD
debates: Whether the bow is a token of mercy here
Whether the bow existed before the flood
How far the vision may be interpreted at all
outliers: Ellicott, Clarke and Wesley take the bow for a token of covenant mercy set against the terrible majesty of the vision; Calvin grants the reading is plausible but holds it unproved, since the whole vision is opposed to it

Calvin denies that the bow was created after the flood, and holds that those who read the promise as meaning it did not exist before distort it, God having inscribed a testimony of favour on a thing not in accordance with it

Clarke declines to interpret the symbolism, asking who can explain its meaning and doubting whether abundant conjectures should be multiplied, and offers only that the whole points to the coming captivity

Ellicott sets the vision in the life of the prophet, who saw it four times, at his call, at the denouncing of judgment, at the departure of the glory from the temple, and at its return in the prophecy of restoration
themes: A rainbow named after a goddess by profane men and after God by Scripture
A bow that is often a sign of continued rain and seems to attract the shower
Colours named one by one and all supposed to be at their utmost perfection
A conqueror shown to be only an instrument
